claims.claim: Gregory Thaumaturgus (c. 213–c. 270); law student turned Origen pupil (233–238); bishop of Neocaesarea.
Thanksgiving Address (c. 238) is his farewell oration and portrait of Origen as teacher.
Gregory Thaumaturgus was born around 213 CE into a wealthy pagan family in Neocaesarea, Pontus (modern day Niksar, Turkey).
Originally named Theodore, he took the name Gregory after his conversion and baptism.
He studied under Origen at Caesarea in Palestine for about five years, probably from 233 to 238 CE.
He and his brother Athenodorus had originally intended to study law at Berytus (modern Beirut) but were diverted to Caesarea when their brother-in-law became imperial governor of Palestine.
The Thanksgiving Address to Origen was delivered as a farewell speech upon Gregory's departure from Palestine at the end of his studies, praising his teacher and expressing gratitude.
The work provides a detailed description of Origen's teaching methods and curriculum, which included logic, geometry, physics, astronomy, ethics, philosophy, ancient literature, and biblical science.
Origen responded to Gregory's Address with a letter of acknowledgment urging him to dedicate himself to church ministry.
Gregory later became bishop of his hometown Neocaesarea, where he died around 270 CE.
The Address is considered one of the most important surviving documents for understanding Origen as a teacher and the nature of Christian education in the third century.
The text survives as part of Gregory's acknowledged writings, though it was not easily accessible until modern critical editions were published.
The work is also known in older scholarship as the Oration and Panegyric Addressed to Origen.
